explanations.explanation: Close, but David says the opposite. His words are, “You are my Lord; apart from You I have no good thing.” No side stash, friend, and no secret shelf of good stuff tucked behind the flour. Apart from God, he says he has none.
Yes, friend. David says, “apart from You I have no good thing.” Not a few, not one. I think that's about the most honest line anybody can say to God, and it fits in a single breath.

That's the one, baker. David says, “As for the saints in the land, they are the excellence in whom all my delight resides.” He names the saints in the land as the ones he delights in. That's a good kind of friend group.
Not this time. The kings of the nations don't show up in this verse. David says the people he delights in are “…the saints in the land…” Those are the ones he names.
Nice guess, but the elders at the gate don't show up in this psalm at all. David says all his delight resides in “…the saints in the land…” I'd have taken a seat at that table for sure.

Right on, friend. David says, “Sorrows will multiply to those who chase other gods.” Notice what's multiplying, and it's not a good batch. I'd take one tray of plain dough over a hundred trays of that.
I get why you'd think so, but David never mentions riches here. He says, “Sorrows will multiply to those who chase other gods.” Something does multiply, just not money.
Nope, no followers in this verse. David says the thing that multiplies is sorrows: “Sorrows will multiply to those who chase other gods.” No fan club, baker. Just sorrows.
That's right. David says he will not “…speak their names with my lips.” He's not saying it quietly or with an eye roll. He just keeps those names off his lips, and that's a firm line.

Careful here, friend, because David does say it. He says he will not pour out their libations of blood “…or speak their names with my lips.” So the names stay out of his mouth. I've had a few recipes I felt that way about.

That's it, baker. David says, “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; You have made my lot secure.” Out of everything he could pick, he picks the LORD. When the Giver is your portion, you're not worried about the size of the slice.
Not this time, baker. The verse says, “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup…” The portion David picks isn't a sword. It's the LORD Himself.
Good thinking, but the verse doesn't say throne. It says, “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup…” That's the pick, friend. No cushion required.

Not quite, friend. David says the opposite: “The lines of my boundary have fallen in pleasant places; surely my inheritance is delightful.” Delightful is the word he uses. This man is not asking for a refund.
Yes, baker. David says, “surely my inheritance is delightful.” He looks at the lines of his boundary and calls them pleasant places. I think that's a man who's glad where he landed.
Right, friend. David says, “I will bless the LORD who counsels me…” He even adds that “even at night my conscience instructs me.” Free advice that doesn't sleep.
I can see the guess, but a crown isn't what David names. The verse says, “I will bless the LORD who counsels me…” It's about advice, not a crown. Counsel is what he says the LORD gives him.
Good try, but rewards aren't what David names here. He says, “I will bless the LORD who counsels me…” The LORD gives him counsel, and David blesses Him for it.

That's the one, baker. David says, “I have set the LORD always before me. Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken.” Hold on, let me say it right: “I have set the LORD always before me.” Then comes “…I will not be shaken.” Steady hands, and that's coming from a stamper with a mustache for arms.

Reasonable guess, but David doesn't say that. He says, “Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken.” Tired is a different thing from shaken. Shaken is about staying put when things get bumpy.
Ha, I'd sign up for that too, but David never says it. He says, “Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken.” Not shaken, friend. The wrinkles are on their own.
Yes, baker. David says, “…my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices…” His heart is glad, and the joy comes right out of his mouth. You can't keep that quiet.
That's it, friend. David says, “my body also will dwell securely.” Not nervously, not by luck. Securely.
Not this one. David says his heart is glad, not heavy. The verse says, “Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices…” A glad heart is light on its feet.
Not quite, baker. David says his heart is glad, and “afraid” isn't in the verse. With the LORD at his right hand, he says he will not be shaken (Psalm 16:8). Afraid just doesn't fit that picture.
Close in sound, but the opposite in meaning. David says his body “…will dwell securely.” No tossing and turning in this verse, friend.
Careful, friend, because David says the opposite. He says, “…nor will You let Your Holy One see decay.” So no decay for God's Holy One. That's a promise, and a big one.

That's right, baker. David says God will not “…let Your Holy One see decay.” Peter, one of Jesus' apostles, later says David looked ahead and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ (Acts 2:31). Big promise, tucked inside one short line.
Yes, friend. David says, “You have made known to me the path of life…” After talking about Sheol and decay, he turns to life. Then he adds, “You will fill me with joy in Your presence…”
Not here, baker. No sea in this verse. David says, “You have made known to me the path of life…” It's a path, but it's a path of life.
Good thought, but the wilderness isn't in this psalm. David says, “You have made known to me the path of life…” No sand in the shoes, friend. Just joy in God's presence.
